fields.title: What is a variable?
fields.content:
Think of a variable like a labeled box.

Imagine you have a box labeled "age" and you put the number 25 inside.
Now, every time you say "age", everyone knows you mean the box with 25 in it.

In Python:
    age = 25

That's it. You just created a variable called age and put 25 inside.

Common mistake:
    =  means "put this in the box"
    == means "is this equal to?"

Try it:
    name = "Christian"
    print(name)
    # Output: Christian

Your turn: Create a variable with your name and print it.

fields.title: Making decisions with if
fields.content:
Imagine you're at a bus stop. If the bus is full, you wait.
If it's empty, you board. That's an "if" statement.

    if bus_is_full:
        wait()
    else:
        board()

Try this:
    age = 20
    if age >= 18:
        print("You can vote!")

Common mistakes:
- Forgetting the colon (:) after if
- Wrong indentation - Python cares about spaces

fields.title: Greetings that work everywhere
fields.content:
Simple greetings for any situation:

Formal:
  "Good morning." / "Good afternoon." / "Good evening."

Casual:
  "Hi!" / "Hey!" / "What's up?"

Friendly and safe:
  "How are you?"  →  "I'm fine, thank you. And you?"

Tip: If you're nervous, start with a smile + "Hi".

fields.title: Your first formula
fields.content:
Excel is a giant calculator.

Every cell has an address like A1, B2, C3.
The letter is the column, the number is the row.

To add two numbers:
1. Click cell A1 → type 5 → press Enter
2. Click cell A2 → type 10 → press Enter
3. Click cell A3 → type =A1+A2 → press Enter

A3 will show 15.

The "=" tells Excel: this is a formula, calculate it.

Try it:
  A1: 100
  A2: 250
  A3: =A1+A2   →  shows 350

That's the start of everything in Excel.

fields.title: Repeating things with loops
fields.content:
Why write the same thing 100 times? Use a loop.

    for i in range(5):
        print("Hello")

That prints "Hello" 5 times.

Try it:
    for name in ["Ada", "Bola", "Chidi"]:
        print(f"Hello, {name}!")

The f before the quote means "fill in the {}".
This is called an f-string.

fields.title: Lists - storing many things
fields.content:
A list holds many values in order.

    fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]

To get the first one:
    fruits[0]   # "apple"

To add a new one:
    fruits.append("orange")

Try it:
    shopping = ["rice", "beans", "oil"]
    shopping.append("tomatoes")
    print(shopping)

Remember: Python starts counting at 0.

fields.title: Functions - reusable blocks
fields.content:
A function is a recipe you can reuse.

    def greet(name):
        print(f"Hello, {name}!")

    greet("Ada")     # Hello, Ada!
    greet("Bola")    # Hello, Bola!

The def keyword means "define a function".

Try it:
    def add(a, b):
        return a + b

    print(add(3, 5))   # 8

The return sends a value back.

fields.title: Dictionaries - labeled data
fields.content:
A dictionary stores data with labels (keys).

    person = {"name": "Ada", "age": 25}

    print(person["name"])   # Ada
    print(person["age"])    # 25

Add a new key:
    person["city"] = "Lagos"

Try it:
    student = {"name": "Chidi", "score": 85}
    print(f"{student['name']} scored {student['score']}")

fields.title: Reading user input
fields.content:
Programs often need input from the user.

    name = input("What's your name? ")
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

Note: input() always returns a string.

If you need a number:
    age = int(input("How old are you? "))

Try it - save as hello.py and run:
    python hello.py

fields.title: Writing your first file
fields.content:
Python can read and write files.

Write a file:
    with open("note.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("Hello, world!")

Read a file:
    with open("note.txt", "r") as f:
        print(f.read())

The "w" means write, "r" means read.
The with keyword closes the file automatically.

fields.title: Errors and how to fix them
fields.content:
Errors are normal - they tell you what's wrong.

Common ones:
    NameError      - you used a name you didn't define
    TypeError      - wrong type (like adding text + number)
    IndentationError - wrong spacing

Example:
    print(age)   # NameError if age isn't defined

Read the last line of the error first - it tells you the problem.

fields.title: What to learn next
fields.content:
You now know the basics! Where to go from here:

1. Practice daily - 10 minutes is enough
2. Build small things - a calculator, a to-do list
3. Read other people's code on GitHub
4. When you get stuck, that's normal. Ask for help.

Soon you'll be teaching someone one step behind you.

That's the StepUp way.

fields.title: Basic math functions
fields.content:
Common formulas:
    =SUM(A1:A10)     adds a range
    =AVERAGE(A1:A10) gets the average
    =MAX(A1:A10)     biggest number
    =MIN(A1:A10)     smallest number

Try it:
    A1: 10
    A2: 20
    A3: 30
    A4: =SUM(A1:A3)   → 60

fields.title: Making your sheet look good
fields.content:
Formatting makes data readable:

Bold: Ctrl+B
Currency: Home → $ icon
Borders: Home → Border icon
Colors: Home → Fill color

Tip: Never use color alone to convey meaning - also use text or borders.

fields.title: Sorting and filtering
fields.content:
Sort a column:
1. Click any cell in the column
2. Data → Sort A→Z or Z→A

Filter to show only some rows:
1. Select your table
2. Data → Filter
3. Click the small arrow → choose what to show

Great for finding the top 10, biggest sales, etc.

fields.title: Freeze panes - keep headers visible
fields.content:
When scrolling, headers disappear. Fix that:

1. Click a cell below the header row
2. View → Freeze Panes → Freeze Panes

Now scrolling keeps the top row visible. Essential for big tables.

fields.title: Charts in 30 seconds
fields.content:
Visualize data fast:

1. Select your data (including headers)
2. Insert → Chart (choose Column, Line, or Pie)
3. Done.

Choose chart type by story:
- Compare values → Column
- Show trend over time → Line
- Show parts of a whole → Pie

fields.title: VLOOKUP - find anything
fields.content:
Need to look up info from a table?

    =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_range, column_number, FALSE)

Example: find the price of "Apple" from a fruit table:
    =VLOOKUP("Apple", A2:C100, 3, FALSE)

FALSE means "exact match" - always use this.

fields.title: IF statements
fields.content:
Make Excel react to values:

    =IF(A1>50, "Pass", "Fail")

Translation: If A1 is greater than 50, show "Pass". Otherwise "Fail".

Nested:
    =IF(A1>=70, "A", IF(A1>=50, "B", "C"))

fields.title: Conditional formatting
fields.content:
Color cells automatically based on rules:

1. Select your numbers
2. Home → Conditional Formatting
3. Choose "Color Scales" or "Data Bars"

Now big numbers turn green, small turn red - at a glance.

fields.title: Saving and sharing
fields.content:
Save your work: Ctrl+S (always!)

Share:
- File → Share → send via email or link
- Or File → Save As → PDF for reports

Pro tip: Save as .xlsx for editing.
Save as .csv if another program needs the raw data.

fields.title: What is ChatGPT (and what it's not)
fields.content:
ChatGPT is a computer program that talks like a person.

It can: write, explain, summarize, translate, brainstorm.
It can't: know everything, always be right, replace your judgment.

Think of it as a very well-read assistant - helpful, but you're in charge.

fields.title: Writing your first prompt
fields.content:
A prompt is what you type to the AI.

Bad prompt:
    "Write something."

Good prompt:
    "Write a 3-paragraph email to my boss asking for Friday off.
     Keep it polite and short."

More detail = better answer.

fields.title: The 4-part prompt formula
fields.content:
Best prompts have 4 parts:

1. Role: "You are a career coach."
2. Task: "Review my CV."
3. Context: "I'm applying for a junior developer job."
4. Format: "Give 5 specific suggestions, numbered."

Example:
    "You are a career coach. Review my CV for a junior developer job.
     Give 5 specific suggestions, numbered."

fields.title: Getting better answers
fields.content:
If the first answer isn't good, don't start over.

Say:
- "Make it shorter."
- "Try again, more formal."
- "Give me 3 more options."
- "Explain it like I'm 10."

Chatting back and forth is how you get great results.

fields.title: Using AI for learning
fields.content:
Great ways to learn with AI:

- "Explain photosynthesis like I'm 12."
- "Quiz me on French verbs."
- "What did I get wrong in this sentence?"
- "Give me 5 practice math problems."

It's like having a patient tutor - free, 24/7.

fields.title: Using AI for writing
fields.content:
AI helps with writing, but always review it.

Good uses:
- Draft an email
- Fix grammar
- Rewrite professionally
- Summarize a long document

Rule: Never send AI writing without reading it first.
The AI doesn't know your boss, your friend, or your tone.

fields.title: AI for work and business
fields.content:
Business uses:

- Write product descriptions
- Draft customer replies
- Brainstorm business names
- Analyze a spreadsheet (paste data, ask questions)
- Translate for international customers

Always fact-check numbers and names.

fields.title: Images, audio, video with AI
fields.content:
AI can also make:

- Images (Midjourney, DALL·E)
- Voice (ElevenLabs)
- Video (Runway, CapCut AI)
- Music (Suno)

Great for: presentations, social media, small business content.

Free tools exist for all of these - start there.

fields.title: Privacy and safety
fields.content:
Never share with AI:
- Passwords
- Bank details
- Other people's private info
- Company secrets

Assume anything you type might be stored.

For personal things, talk to a human - not an AI.

fields.title: AI won't replace you
fields.content:
AI won't replace you. But a person using AI well
might replace someone who doesn't.

Use AI to:
- Save time on boring tasks
- Learn faster
- Do work you couldn't do alone

Your judgment, taste, and relationships are still yours.

fields.title: Your home screen and apps
fields.content:
Your home screen shows apps as icons.

- Tap an app to open it.
- Swipe left/right to see more screens.
- The back button (◁) or swipe from left edge → go back.
- The home button → return to home screen.

Don't worry about breaking anything. You can't.

fields.title: Making calls and sending texts
fields.content:
To call:
1. Open Phone app
2. Type the number or pick from contacts
3. Tap green call button

To text:
1. Open Messages
2. Tap +, choose contact
3. Type your message → send arrow

Tip: Add contacts you call often. Saves time.

fields.title: Using WhatsApp
fields.content:
WhatsApp is for messaging with internet (free).

- Chats: 1-to-1 or group messages
- Voice notes: hold the mic 🎤 to record
- Video calls: tap the camera icon
- Photos: tap 📎 to send images

End-to-end encrypted - only you and the receiver see messages.

fields.title: Taking and sharing photos
fields.content:
Open the Camera app.

- Tap the round button to take a photo
- Switch front/back camera (⇄ icon)
- Video: swipe to "Video" mode, tap record

Share:
1. Open the photo in your gallery
2. Tap Share → choose WhatsApp/email/etc.

fields.title: Managing storage
fields.content:
Phone full? Try this:

1. Photos → back up to Google Photos → delete from phone
2. Delete videos you don't need
3. Settings → Apps → uninstall unused apps
4. Settings → Storage → clear cache for big apps

Free up 1-5 GB this way.

fields.title: Battery saving
fields.content:
Make your battery last longer:

- Turn off Bluetooth and WiFi when not needed
- Lower screen brightness
- Close apps you're not using
- Use Battery Saver mode

Charge before it hits 20% - better for battery health.

fields.title: Staying safe from scams
fields.content:
Common scams:
- "You won a prize - send money to claim"
- "Your bank account is locked - click this link"
- "I love you - send me money" (romance scam)

Rule: If it feels too good or urgent - it's a scam.
Never send money or share passwords.

fields.title: Backing up your data
fields.content:
Back up so you don't lose everything.

Android: Settings → Google → Backup → Back up now
iPhone: Settings → [your name] → iCloud → iCloud Backup → On

Do it monthly. Takes a few minutes.

fields.title: Using maps to get around
fields.content:
Google Maps is your GPS.

- Type destination → tap Directions
- Choose walking/driving/transit
- Blue dot shows you
- Tap mic to speak destination

Download offline maps:
1. Search city
2. Tap bottom info → Download
3. Works without internet!

fields.title: Digital payments safely
fields.content:
Mobile money / banking apps:

Safe habits:
- Use a screen lock (PIN, fingerprint)
- Never share your PIN
- Log out after use in public
- Check SMS alerts for every transaction

If something looks wrong, call your bank - not the number in an SMS.

fields.title: Introducing yourself
fields.content:
Keep it short and warm.

    "Hi, I'm Ada. Nice to meet you."
    "Hello, my name is Chidi. What's your name?"

If they ask "Where are you from?":
    "I'm from Nigeria."
    "I'm from Lagos, but I live in Abuja now."

That's all you need. Don't overthink it.

fields.title: Small talk - safe topics
fields.content:
Safe topics:
- Weather: "It's so hot today, isn't it?"
- Weekend: "Do anything nice this weekend?"
- Food: "Have you eaten lunch yet?"
- Work/school: "How's work going?"

Avoid: money, politics, religion, personal questions.

fields.title: Asking for help politely
fields.content:
Start with:
    "Excuse me, could you help me?"

Then explain:
    "I'm looking for the train station."
    "Could you tell me where the bathroom is?"

Always end with:
    "Thank you so much."
    "I really appreciate it."

fields.title: Ordering food
fields.content:
In a restaurant:

    "Could I have the chicken and rice, please?"
    "Can I get a bottle of water?"
    "Excuse me - could we get the bill?"

Say "please" and "thank you" - they matter everywhere.

fields.title: Talking about your day
fields.content:
Practice past tense naturally:

    "I woke up early today."
    "I had a long meeting."
    "Then I went to the market."
    "After that, I cooked dinner."

Use "then", "after that", "later" to tell a story.

fields.title: Making plans
fields.content:
Ask:
    "Are you free on Saturday?"
    "Do you want to grab coffee?"

Reply yes:
    "Yes, sounds great!"

Reply no politely:
    "I'm sorry, I can't. Maybe next time?"

Suggest:
    "How about 3pm?"
    "Does Sunday work for you?"

fields.title: Apologizing and fixing mistakes
fields.content:
If you make a mistake:

    "I'm so sorry - that was my fault."
    "I apologize for the misunderstanding."

Fix it:
    "Let me make it right."
    "How can I fix this?"

A good apology is short, honest, and has a fix.

fields.title: Phone and video calls
fields.content:
Starting:
    "Hello, this is Ada speaking."
    "Hi, is this a good time to talk?"

Ending:
    "Thanks for your time. Talk soon!"
    "Have a great day!"

On video: mute when not talking. Look at the camera, not yourself.

fields.title: Confidence - speaking without fear
fields.content:
Everyone makes mistakes. Even native speakers.

Rule 1: Speak slowly. Slow is better than fast-and-wrong.
Rule 2: If you don't know a word, describe it.
    "The thing you use to cut paper..." → scissors
Rule 3: Practice out loud every day. 5 minutes.
Rule 4: Smile. People want you to succeed.

fields.title: Bonjour! Saying hello
fields.content:

In 3 months, you'll be shocked how far you've come.

fields.title: What is a fraction?
fields.content:
A fraction is part of a whole.

  1/2 means: one piece out of two equal pieces.
  The top number (1) = numerator   → how many pieces you have
  The bottom (2) = denominator    → how many pieces total

Picture a pizza cut into 4 slices. You eat 1 slice → 1/4.

fields.title: Equivalent fractions
fields.content:
Same value, different look.

  1/2  =  2/4  =  3/6  =  50/100

Rule: multiply top AND bottom by the same number.

  1/2 × 2/2 = 2/4

Multiply top only? Wrong. Always both.

fields.title: Adding fractions (same bottom)
fields.content:
When denominators match, just add the tops.

  1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5

Denominator stays the same. Think: 1 slice + 2 slices = 3 slices.

fields.title: Adding fractions (different bottom)
fields.content:
Different denominators? Find a common one.

  1/2 + 1/3

Common denominator is 6:
  1/2 = 3/6
  1/3 = 2/6
  3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6

Method: find LCM of the two bottoms.

fields.title: Subtracting fractions
fields.content:
Same idea as adding.

  3/4 − 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2

Different denominators?
  1/2 − 1/3 = 3/6 − 2/6 = 1/6

fields.title: Multiplying fractions
fields.content:
Multiply straight across - top × top, bottom × bottom.

  2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15

No common denominator needed!

fields.title: Dividing fractions
fields.content:
Flip the second fraction and multiply.

  1/2 ÷ 1/4  =  1/2 × 4/1  =  4/2  =  2

Remember: "Keep, Change, Flip"
  Keep the first fraction
  Change ÷ to ×
  Flip the second fraction

fields.title: What is a decimal?
fields.content:
A decimal is another way to write a fraction.

  1/2 = 0.5
  1/4 = 0.25
  3/4 = 0.75

The dot separates whole numbers from parts.
  2.75 = 2 wholes + 0.75

fields.title: Converting fractions ↔ decimals
fields.content:
Fraction → Decimal: divide the top by the bottom.
  3/4 = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75

Decimal → Fraction:
  0.5 = 5/10 = 1/2
  0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4

Write the decimal over 10, 100, 1000... then simplify.

fields.title: Real-life fractions
fields.content:
Where you use fractions daily:

- Cooking: 1/2 cup of rice
- Shopping: 1/3 off sale
- Time: quarter past 3 (1/4 hour)
- Money: 25 cents = 1/4 of a dollar

Practice: next shopping trip, calculate discounts in your head.

fields.title: What is algebra?
fields.content:
Algebra uses letters to represent unknown numbers.

  x + 3 = 7

What number plus 3 equals 7? x = 4.

Letters are placeholders. Once you find the value, you've "solved for x".

fields.title: Solving simple equations
fields.content:
Rule: whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

  x + 5 = 12
  x + 5 − 5 = 12 − 5
  x = 7

The goal: get x alone on one side.

fields.title: The order of operations (PEMDAS)
fields.content:
Follow this order:
  P - Parentheses ( )
  E - Exponents (²)
  M/D - Multiply & Divide (left to right)
  A/S - Add & Subtract (left to right)

Example:
  2 + 3 × 4 = 2 + 12 = 14   (multiply first!)

Not: (2+3) × 4 = 20 - that's only if parentheses are there.

fields.title: Negative numbers
fields.content:
Rules to remember:

  (−) + (−) = more negative     −3 + −2 = −5
  (+) + (−) = subtract         5 + (−3) = 2
  (−) × (−) = positive         (−3) × (−4) = 12
  (−) × (+) = negative         (−3) × 4 = −12

Two negatives make a positive - only when multiplying/dividing.

fields.title: Variables on both sides
fields.content:
2x + 3 = x + 7

Move x's to one side:
  2x − x + 3 = 7
  x + 3 = 7
  x = 4

Get all the x's together. Then solve normally.

fields.title: Distributive property
fields.content:
a(b + c) = ab + ac

Example:
  3(x + 4) = 3x + 12

Multiply what's outside by each term inside.

fields.title: Solving with fractions
fields.content:
x/3 + 2 = 5

Step 1: Subtract 2 from both sides.
  x/3 = 3

Step 2: Multiply both sides by 3.
  x = 9

To undo division, multiply. To undo multiplication, divide.

fields.title: Word problems
fields.content:
Translate words into equations:

  "5 more than a number" → x + 5
  "3 times a number"     → 3x
  "Half of a number"     → x/2

Example:
  "The sum of 3 times a number and 5 is 20."
  → 3x + 5 = 20
  → 3x = 15
  → x = 5

fields.title: Graphing simple equations
fields.content:
y = 2x + 1

Pick x values and find y:
  x=0 → y=1
  x=1 → y=3
  x=2 → y=5

Plot the points and connect them → straight line.

Slope = 2 (line goes up 2 for every 1 right)
Intercept = 1 (crosses y-axis at 1)

fields.title: Why algebra matters
fields.content:
Algebra is the language of patterns.

You'll use it for:
- Calculating bills and interest
- Programming (every code uses variables)
- Science (physics, chemistry, biology)
- Business decisions (profit, cost, price)

Once it clicks, it unlocks everything else.

fields.title: What a CV is really for
fields.content:
A CV has one job: get you an interview. Not the job - the interview.

That means:
- Recruiters spend 6-10 seconds on it
- It must be scannable in seconds
- Every word must earn its place

Think: newspaper ad, not diary.

fields.title: The one-page rule
fields.content:
For under 10 years of experience: ONE page.

For over 10 years or academic roles: two pages max.

Why?
- Recruiters don't read - they scan
- Long CVs hide your best stuff
- Concise = confident

Cut ruthlessly. If it doesn't help, delete it.

fields.title: The winning structure
fields.content:
Top-to-bottom order:

1. Name + contact (email, phone, city, LinkedIn)
2. Short professional summary (2-3 lines)
3. Experience (most recent first)
4. Skills
5. Education
6. (Optional) Projects, certifications, languages

Simple. No photos (unless required in your country). No age. No marital status.

fields.title: Writing a killer summary
fields.content:
3 lines at the top that sell you.

Formula:
  [Who you are] + [What you do] + [Your best proof]

Example:
  "Junior web developer with 2 years building Django apps.
   Delivered 8 client projects on time.
   Passionate about clean code and user-focused design."

No: "Hardworking team player seeking opportunities."

fields.title: The experience section - bullets that win
fields.content:
Formula for every bullet:

  [Action verb] + [What you did] + [Result/Number]

Bad:
  "Responsible for managing social media."

Good:
  "Grew Instagram following from 500 to 12,000 in 6 months
   by launching daily behind-the-scenes content."

Numbers > adjectives. Always.

fields.title: Action verbs to use (and avoid)
fields.content:
Strong verbs:
  Led, Built, Grew, Designed, Launched, Reduced,
  Increased, Delivered, Managed, Created, Improved

Weak verbs (avoid):
  Responsible for, Helped with, Worked on,
  Assisted in, Involved in

Start every bullet with a strong verb. No "I".

fields.title: Skills section - what to list
fields.content:
Split into two groups:

Technical: Python, Excel, Photoshop, SQL, Canva

Soft: Leadership, Communication, Problem-solving

List 8-12 max. Don't list things you can't discuss in an interview.

Skip: "Microsoft Word" (everyone knows it). Include only if the job explicitly asks.

fields.title: Tailor for every job
fields.content:
The #1 mistake: sending the same CV to everyone.

For each application:
1. Read the job description twice
2. Highlight 5 keywords they use
3. Make sure those words appear in your CV
4. Reorder bullets to lead with what they need

10 minutes of tailoring > 100 applications.

fields.title: Design that actually works
fields.content:
Formatting rules:

- Font: Calibri, Arial, or Helvetica (readable)
- Size: 10-12pt body, 14-18pt name
- Margins: 2cm
- White space: your friend - don't cram
- Bold for job titles and section headers
- No colors, no photos, no fancy graphics (unless you're a designer)

Save as PDF. Always.

fields.title: Common mistakes that kill CVs
fields.content:
Instant rejection triggers:

❌ Typos or spelling errors
❌ Inconsistent dates or formatting
❌ "References available on request" (obvious)
❌ Gaps without explanation
❌ Fake achievements (they'll ask)
❌ Generic summary ("seeking a challenging role")
❌ Applying with the same CV everywhere

Fix these → your response rate doubles.

fields.title: Why budgets fail
fields.content:
Most budgets fail because they're too strict, too complex,
or based on money you don't actually have.

The fix:
- Start with what you actually earn
- Track for 30 days before changing anything
- Make it simple (one page, one app, one number)

A boring budget you follow beats a perfect one you abandon.

fields.title: The 50/30/20 rule
fields.content:
A simple starting framework:

  50% - Needs (rent, food, transport, bills)
  30% - Wants (eating out, clothes, entertainment)
  20% - Savings & debt repayment

Not perfect for everyone, but a great starting point.

If you can't hit 20% savings yet, aim for 5% then grow it 1% at a time.

fields.title: Track every naira for 30 days
fields.content:
For one month, write down EVERY expense.

Use: notebook, phone notes, or apps like Wallet by BudgetBakers.

At the end of 30 days, you'll see:
- Where money actually goes (surprise!)
- What to cut first
- What you can't believe you spent

Do this before setting any budget. Data > guessing.

fields.title: Build a starter emergency fund
fields.content:
Before investing, save 1 month of expenses in cash.

Why: so one broken phone or medical bill doesn't destroy you.

How:
- Open a separate savings account
- Automate a transfer every payday
- Don't touch it unless truly an emergency

Once you hit 1 month, aim for 3, then 6.

fields.title: Cut without suffering
fields.content:
Big wins first:

1. Subscriptions you forgot (check bank statement)
2. Eating out - cut 30%, not 100%
3. Transport - carpool, walk short trips
4. Phone plan - switch to cheaper data
5. Rent - can you negotiate or move?

Small wins matter, but big bills matter more.

fields.title: Pay off debt smartly
fields.content:
Two methods:

Snowball:
- Pay minimum on all
- Put extra on smallest debt
- When it clears, roll to next

Avalanche:
- Pay minimum on all
- Put extra on highest-interest debt first

Snowball = motivation. Avalanche = math. Pick what works for you.

Always pay minimums. Never miss one.

fields.title: Save for irregular expenses
fields.content:
Big expenses that catch people off guard:

- Rent advance (3-6 months upfront)
- School fees
- Weddings / funerals
- Car repairs / insurance
- Holidays

Plan: divide the annual cost by 12. Save that monthly.
  Annual car insurance ₦120,000 → save ₦10,000/month.

fields.title: Automate everything
fields.content:
Your future self is lazy. So is your present self.

Setup (once, then forget):
- Payday → automatic transfer to savings
- Bills → auto-debit
- Investments → auto-buy monthly

You can't spend money that's already moved.

fields.title: Investing basics
fields.content:
Rules:
1. Only invest money you won't need for 5+ years
2. Diversify (don't put all in one thing)
3. Low fees matter a LOT over time
4. Ignore hot tips - do your own research

In Nigeria: treasury bills, mutual funds, index funds, real estate.
Start small. Consistency beats size.

Never invest in something you don't understand.

fields.title: Review every month
fields.content:
15 minutes on the last day of the month:

- Did I stay within budget?
- What surprised me?
- What should I adjust next month?

Budgets evolve. What worked in January may not in July.
Track → Review → Adjust. Repeat forever.

fields.title: The 5 things every cook must know
fields.content:
1. Read the recipe first (all the way)
2. Prep everything before you start (mise en place)
3. Taste as you go
4. Salt in layers, not at the end
5. Clean as you cook

These five rules separate cooks from chefs.

fields.title: Knife basics
fields.content:
You only need one good knife (8-inch chef's knife).

Basic cuts:
- Dice: small cubes
- Julienne: thin sticks
- Chop: rough pieces
- Mince: very small

Safety:
- Curl fingers under (claw grip)
- Sharp knife > dull knife (dull slips)
- Cut on a wooden or plastic board, never glass

fields.title: Rice that never fails
fields.content:
Perfect rice every time:

1. Rinse rice until water runs clear (removes starch)
2. 1 cup rice : 2 cups water
3. Bring to boil, add salt
4. Cover, lowest heat, 15 minutes
5. OFF the heat, sit 5 more minutes
6. Fluff with fork, never stir

Never lift the lid while cooking.

fields.title: Eggs - 5 ways
fields.content:
Boiled:
  6 min = soft, 10 min = hard. Ice bath after.

Fried:
  Medium heat, butter/oil, 2 min each side.

Scrambled:
  Low heat, stir constantly, remove before fully set.

Omelette:
  Beat, pour, fold when edges set.

Poached:
  Boiling water + splash of vinegar, swirl, drop egg in, 3 min.

fields.title: Cooking protein (meat, chicken, fish)
fields.content:
Golden rules:

- Pat dry before cooking (wet meat steams, doesn't brown)
- Salt 15-30 min before cooking
- Get the pan HOT before adding meat
- Don't move it - let it brown (Maillard reaction = flavor)
- Rest meat 5 min before cutting (juices redistribute)

Chicken: cook to 74°C / 165°F internal
Fish: flakes easily with fork = done
Beef: depends on cut, 55-70°C for medium

fields.title: Vegetables that taste good
fields.content:
Roasting: 200°C, olive oil, salt. 20-30 min. Sweet and deep.

Sautéing: high heat, quick, keep them crisp.

Steaming: preserves nutrients, clean taste.

Boiling: only for potatoes, corn, some greens. Don't overcook.

Rule: Vegetables should be colorful, not grey.

fields.title: Seasoning like a pro
fields.content:
Salt is #1. Everything else builds on it.

Layers of flavor:
1. Salt - brings out natural taste
2. Acid (lemon, vinegar) - brightness
3. Fat (oil, butter) - richness
4. Heat (pepper, chili) - kick
5. Herbs/spices - character

Always taste before serving. Then taste again.

fields.title: Sauces that go with anything
fields.content:
Tomato sauce:
  Onion + garlic + tomatoes + salt + basil. Simmer 30 min.

Pepper sauce:
  Blend peppers, onion, tomato. Fry in oil. 20 min.

White sauce:
  Butter + flour + milk. Whisk. Salt + pepper.

Pesto:
  Blend basil + nuts + garlic + oil + parmesan.

Each sauce takes any dish from plain to special.

fields.title: Meal prep for the week
fields.content:
Sunday 2-hour prep saves 10+ hours:

- Cook a big pot of rice (refrigerate in portions)
- Roast a tray of vegetables
- Cook chicken/beans
- Chop onions, peppers, ginger; freeze in bags
- Make 2 sauces

Then weekdays = assemble, not cook. Dinner in 15 min.

fields.title: Cooking for one (or a family)
fields.content:
For one:
- Cook once, eat 3 times (leftovers are gold)
- Invest in good containers
- Learn 5 dishes you love, rotate them

For family:
- Double every recipe (same effort, half the cost per plate)
- Get everyone involved in the kitchen
- Batch-cook on weekends

Cooking is a life skill. The more you do it, the easier it gets.

fields.title: The DR ABC of first aid
fields.content:
Before you do anything, remember:

  D - Danger (is the scene safe? Protect yourself first)
  R - Response (is the person awake? Shout "Are you OK?")
  A - Airway (is it clear? Tilt head, lift chin)
  B - Breathing (look, listen, feel for 10 seconds)
  C - CPR (if not breathing, start compressions)

This is the universal emergency checklist. Learn it.

fields.title: Calling for emergency help
fields.content:
In Nigeria: 112 (works nationwide for emergencies)

When you call, say:
1. Your location (landmarks help)
2. What happened
3. How many people are hurt
4. The condition of the person

Stay on the line. Follow their instructions.
Don't hang up until they say so.

fields.title: CPR - saving someone's life
fields.content:
Only if the person is NOT breathing.

Adult CPR:
1. Place heel of one hand on center of chest
2. Other hand on top, fingers interlocked
3. Push HARD and FAST - 100-120 per minute
4. Depth: 5-6 cm
5. Don't stop until help arrives or person wakes

Song trick: "Stayin' Alive" by Bee Gees is exactly the right tempo.

Push. Don't be afraid - they're already unconscious.

fields.title: Choking - adults and children
fields.content:
Adult/child choking:

1. Ask: "Are you choking?" (if they can talk, they're not fully choking)
2. If yes: 5 back blows between shoulder blades
3. Then 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver)
4. Repeat until object comes out

For babies (<1 year):
- 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts (not abdominal)

Never put fingers in the throat blindly - you may push it deeper.

fields.title: Bleeding - stopping it fast
fields.content:
1. Apply firm direct pressure with clean cloth
2. Don't lift to check - hold 5-10 min
3. If bleeding through, add another cloth on top (don't remove the first)
4. Elevate the limb above the heart if possible
5. Call for help if bleeding won't stop

For deep cuts with embedded object: DON'T remove it. Stabilize around it.

fields.title: Burns - what to do
fields.content:
For small burns:

1. Cool running water for 10-20 minutes (not ice!)
2. Remove rings/watch from burned area (before swelling)
3. Cover loosely with clean, non-stick cloth
4. Don't pop blisters
5. Don't use butter, toothpaste, or oil

Go to hospital if:
- Burn is bigger than the palm of the hand
- On face, hands, feet, or joints
- White, brown, or charred skin
- Caused by electricity or chemicals

fields.title: Fractures and sprains
fields.content:
If you suspect a broken bone:

1. Don't move the person (unless in danger)
2. Immobilize the injured area (splint with cloth + stick)
3. Apply ice wrapped in cloth for sprains
4. Elevate if possible
5. Get medical help

Signs of fracture: severe pain, deformity, can't move, swelling
Signs of sprain: pain, swelling, bruising but no deformity

fields.title: Fainting and shock
fields.content:
Fainting:
1. Lay person flat
2. Raise legs 30cm above heart
3. Loosen tight clothing
4. Fresh air, cool cloth on forehead
5. They should wake in 1-2 min

Shock (after accident/bleeding):
- Pale, cold, clammy skin
- Rapid weak pulse
- Confusion, thirst

Do: lay flat, keep warm, don't give food/drink, get help fast.

fields.title: Seizures
fields.content:
When someone has a seizure:

DO:
- Clear hard objects around them
- Cushion their head
- Turn on side (recovery position) after
- Time the seizure
- Stay calm, stay with them

DON'T:
- Hold them down
- Put anything in their mouth
- Give water during

Call emergency if seizure lasts >5 min or it's their first one.

fields.title: Building a home first aid kit
fields.content:
Every home needs:

- Adhesive bandages (various sizes)
- Gauze pads + medical tape
- Antiseptic (Dettol, iodine)
- Pain relief (paracetamol)
- Thermometer
- Scissors + tweezers
- Gloves (latex)
- Oral rehydration salts (ORS)
- Cotton wool
- Triangular bandage

Store in a clean, dry, easy-to-reach place.
Check expiration dates every 6 months.

fields.title: Anyone can learn to draw
fields.content:
Drawing is a skill, not a talent.

The myth: some people are "born artists."
The truth: drawing is like writing - anyone can learn with practice.

Start today with a pencil and any paper. That's it.
Your first drawings will be bad. Everyone's are. Keep going.

fields.title: Tools you actually need
fields.content:
To start:
- A pencil (HB or 2B)
- Paper (any)
- An eraser

That's it. Really.

Later you might add:
- Blending stump
- Different pencils (2H to 6B)
- Sketchbook

Expensive tools don't make better art. Practice does.

fields.title: Drawing basic shapes
fields.content:
Everything is made of 4 shapes:

- Sphere (circle)
- Cube (square)
- Cylinder (rounded rectangle)
- Cone (triangle)

A face = oval + circle + 2 cylinders + 2 spheres
A hand = rectangle + 5 cylinders
A tree = cylinder + sphere

Train your eye to see shapes inside everything.

fields.title: Holding your pencil correctly
fields.content:
Two grips - use both:

1. Writing grip (like a pen):
   - For details, small work
   - Firm control

2. Overhand grip:
   - For sketching, shading
   - Freer motion

Start with overhand for the rough sketch.
Switch to writing grip for details.

fields.title: Lines and strokes
fields.content:
Practice these daily for 5 minutes:

- Straight lines (all directions)
- Curved lines (smooth arcs)
- Circles (small to large)
- Hatching (parallel lines)
- Cross-hatching (overlapping lines)

Confident lines > perfect lines.
Draw from your shoulder, not your wrist.

fields.title: Light and shadow - the magic
fields.content:
Everything you draw has:

1. Highlight (brightest spot)
2. Mid-tone (base color)
3. Shadow (dark side)
4. Cast shadow (on the ground)
5. Reflected light (bounce)

Draw the shadow shapes BEFORE shading.
Shadow does 80% of the work for realism.

fields.title: Perspective - making things look 3D
fields.content:
One-point perspective:

1. Draw a horizon line
2. Place a dot (vanishing point)
3. Draw lines from the dot outward
4. Everything shrinks toward the dot

Practice: draw a road, a room, a hallway.

Two-point perspective: two dots on the horizon.
Used for corners of buildings.

This is the secret to realistic depth.

fields.title: Drawing faces
fields.content:
Face proportions (front view):

- Head is an oval
- Eyes at the middle of the head (not top!)
- 5 eyes fit across the face width
- Nose halfway between eyes and chin
- Mouth halfway between nose and chin
- Ears from eyes to nose level

Draw these guidelines lightly. Then build the face.

fields.title: Shading techniques
fields.content:
Four ways to shade:

1. Smooth (blending with finger or stump) - soft, realistic
2. Hatching (parallel lines) - sketchy, energetic
3. Cross-hatching (grid of lines) - dense, textured
4. Stippling (dots) - patient, illustrative

Pick one and master it. Then learn the next.

Whatever you choose - build layers slowly. Don't press hard.

fields.title: Daily practice plan
fields.content:
15 minutes a day beats 2 hours once a week.

Weekly plan:
- Mon: 15 min lines and shapes
- Tue: 15 min still life (cup, fruit)
- Wed: 15 min a face from reference
- Thu: 15 min hands (hard - do them anyway)
- Fri: 15 min something from imagination
- Sat: 30 min finish a piece
- Sun: rest or doodle freely

In 3 months, you won't recognize your own work.

fields.title: Why CapCut (and not Premiere)
fields.content:
CapCut is FREE, fast, and mobile-first.

Why it's perfect for beginners:
- Works on phone and desktop
- Templates for instant results
- Auto-captions, auto-beats
- Exports in 4K
- No watermarks on mobile (currently)

Professionals use Premiere. Creators use CapCut.
Start here. Level up later if needed.

fields.title: Your first 60-second edit
fields.content:
The simple flow:

1. Open CapCut → New Project
2. Select video clips from your phone
3. Tap "+" to add them to timeline
4. Trim: drag edges of each clip to shorten
5. Add music: Audio → pick track
6. Add text: Text → type + style
7. Export

That's a real video. Post it. You just edited.

fields.title: Trimming like a pro
fields.content:
Rule: cut every "um" and dead second.

The 3 cuts you'll use most:
1. Jump cut - remove middle of a talking clip
2. B-roll cut - cut to showing what you're saying
3. Beat cut - cut on the beat of the music

The first 3 seconds decide if someone watches.
Cut to the good part immediately.

fields.title: Adding music that works
fields.content:
Music = 50% of a video's feel.

Sources (free):
- CapCut's built-in library
- YouTube Audio Library
- Pixabay Music
- Free Music Archive

Match genre:
- Action → fast, drums
- Emotional → soft, piano
- Funny → quirky, upbeat
- Tutorial → calm, low-key

Auto-beat feature: CapCut can cut video to the beat - use it!

fields.title: Text and captions
fields.content:
80% of people watch with sound off. Captions are required.

Auto-captions in CapCut:
1. Text → Auto Captions → Detect
2. Fix any wrong words
3. Style: white text, black outline, bold
4. Position: center bottom

Text styles that work:
- Karaoke (words pop as spoken)
- Typewriter (letters appear)
- Big bold (headers)

Keep font readable. No fancy cursive.

fields.title: Transitions and effects
fields.content:
Transitions between clips:

- Cut (no transition) - 90% of the time
- Fade - soft, calm
- Zoom - energetic
- Slide - casual

Rule: use transitions SPARINGLY. Cutting is fine.

Effects to know:
- Speed (slow-mo or speed-up)
- Reverse (play backward)
- Zoom in/out (build drama)

Don't overdo - effects shouldn't distract.

fields.title: Color and filters
fields.content:
CapCut has one-tap filters.

Common looks:
- Warm (orange tint) - cozy, friendly
- Cool (blue tint) - cinematic, serious
- Vintage - nostalgic
- High contrast - bold, punchy

Adjust manually:
- Brightness (overall light)
- Contrast (light vs dark)
- Saturation (color intensity)
- Temperature (warm vs cool)

Slight adjustments. Don't over-edit.

fields.title: Creating Reels/TikToks that perform
fields.content:
Vertical, 9:16, under 60 seconds.

Winning formula:
- Hook in first 1 second (surprising image or text)
- Fast pacing (cut every 2-3 seconds)
- Captions always on
- Trending audio (check the app)
- Loop-worthy ending (watch again)

Don't: start slow, no music, no captions, 3-minute videos.

fields.title: Longer videos (YouTube style)
fields.content:
Structure:

0:00-0:15 - Hook ("Today I'll show you...")
0:15-0:30 - Intro + what they'll get
0:30-X:XX - Main content (chapters help)
Last 30 sec - Recap + subscribe CTA

Chapters (YouTube):
1. Description → type 0:00 Intro, 1:30 Chapter 2, etc.
2. YouTube auto-creates clickable chapters

Keep intro short. Get to value fast.

fields.title: Exporting for each platform
fields.content:
Settings matter:

YouTube: 1080p or 4K, 16:9 landscape
TikTok/Reels/Shorts: 1080×1920, 9:16 vertical
WhatsApp status: 1080×1920, under 30 sec
Instagram feed: 1080×1350 (4:5)

Export at the HIGHEST quality CapCut allows.
Higher bitrate = crisper video.

File size too big? Re-export at 720p - still fine for most.

fields.title: What stress actually is
fields.content:
Stress is your body's response to a challenge.

Short-term: sharpens focus, gives energy (good!)
Long-term: damages sleep, immunity, heart, brain

It's not "in your head" - it's real chemistry.
Cortisol and adrenaline do physical damage over months.

The goal isn't zero stress. It's managing it.

fields.title: The 4-7-8 breathing trick
fields.content:
The fastest way to calm your nervous system:

1. Breathe in through nose for 4 seconds
2. Hold for 7 seconds
3. Breathe out through mouth for 8 seconds
4. Repeat 4 times

Why it works: long exhale = parasympathetic activation.
Do it anywhere - desk, bus, bed.

Feeling panic? This stops it in 2 minutes.

fields.title: The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique
fields.content:
For anxiety and overwhelm:

Look around and name:
  5 things you can SEE
  4 things you can TOUCH
  3 things you can HEAR
  2 things you can SMELL
  1 thing you can TASTE

This drags your brain out of the spiral and into the room.
Works in 60 seconds.

fields.title: Sleep - your #1 stress medicine
fields.content:
Rules for sleep:

- Same bedtime every day (yes, weekends too)
- No screens 1 hour before bed
- Cool, dark, quiet room
- No caffeine after 2pm
- Bed is for sleep (not for scrolling)

If you can't sleep after 20 min: get up, do something calm, try again.

7-9 hours. Non-negotiable.

fields.title: Move your body
fields.content:
Exercise destroys stress hormones.

The minimum:
- 20-minute walk daily
- Or 10 minutes of stretching
- Or dancing to 3 songs

You don't need a gym. You need to move.

Even better: sunlight + walking = double benefit.

Feeling overwhelmed? Walk first, think later.

fields.title: Write it out (journaling)
fields.content:
When your mind spins, put it on paper.

Morning pages (10 minutes):
- Write 3 pages by hand, whatever comes
- No editing, no judging
- Just clear the mental clutter

Or: at night, write 3 things that went well.
Trains your brain to notice the good.

fields.title: Set boundaries without guilt
fields.content:
Saying yes to everything = stress factory.

Scripts that help:
- "I can't take that on right now."
- "Let me check my schedule and get back to you."
- "I need to say no this time."

No is a full sentence. You don't owe an explanation.

Protect your time like it's money. Because it is.

fields.title: Talk to someone
fields.content:
Stress + isolation = worse.

Talk to:
- A trusted friend
- Family member
- Therapist or counselor
- Support group
- Even a helpline

You don't need to be "in crisis" to ask for help.
Talking once a week prevents crisis.

If in Nigeria: SURPIN (suicide prevention) 08062106493
Or find a local mental health helpline.

fields.title: Reduce input (social media detox)
fields.content:
Modern stress often comes from:

- Endless news
- Doom scrolling
- Comparing your life to filtered highlights

Try this week:
- Delete one social app from phone for 7 days
- Or: only check it 1 hour/day
- Mute 5 accounts that make you feel bad
- Follow 5 that teach or uplift

Your brain will thank you.

fields.title: When to get professional help
fields.content:
Red flags that need a professional:

- Can't sleep for 2+ weeks
- Can't eat, or eating too much
- Losing interest in everything
- Thoughts of self-harm
- Panic attacks weekly
- Alcohol/drugs to cope
- Can't work or function

This is not weakness. It's like a broken arm - get it treated.

Therapy works. Medication works. Both together work best.

Asking for help is a strength move.

fields.title: Why home workouts work
fields.content:
Gyms cost money and time. Home workouts:

- 15-30 min per session
- No equipment (or a mat)
- No commute
- No judgement
- Free forever

Consistency beats intensity. 3 short sessions/week beats 1 gym day.

fields.title: The 5 movement patterns
fields.content:
Every workout should hit these:

1. Squat (stand up and down)
2. Hinge (bend at hips, back straight)
3. Push (pushups, dips)
4. Pull (rows with a towel or bag)
5. Carry (walking with weight)

Train all 5 each week. Ignore the rest for now.

fields.title: The perfect warm-up (5 min)
fields.content:
Never skip it. Prevents injury.

1. March in place - 1 min
2. Arm circles - 30 sec each direction
3. Hip circles - 30 sec each direction
4. Bodyweight squats - 10 reps
5. Inchworms - 5 reps
6. Jumping jacks - 30 sec

Done. Now you're ready.

fields.title: Pushups - from zero to 20
fields.content:
Can't do one? Start here:

Week 1: Wall pushups - 3 sets of 10
Week 2: Incline pushups (hands on chair) - 3×10
Week 3: Knee pushups - 3×5
Week 4: Regular pushups - 3×3
Week 5+: Add reps every week

Form: hands under shoulders, body straight, core tight.
Chest to floor (or almost).

fields.title: Squats - the king of exercises
fields.content:
Works your whole lower body.

Proper form:
- Feet shoulder-width apart
- Toes slightly out
- Sit back like there's a chair behind you
- Knees track over toes (not collapsing in)
- Chest up, back straight
- Go as low as comfortable (aim for thighs parallel)

Beginner: 3 sets × 10 reps
Rest 60 sec between sets.

Progress: add 2 reps/week, or slow down (3-second down).

fields.title: Core - the plank
fields.content:
Forget crunches. Planks are better.

Basics:
- Elbows under shoulders
- Body straight from head to heels
- Squeeze abs, glutes, thighs
- Breathe normally

Hold 20 seconds. Rest 20. Repeat 3 times.

Weekly: add 5 seconds.

Variations once 60 sec is easy:
- Side plank
- Plank with shoulder taps
- Plank with leg lifts

fields.title: The 15-minute full-body routine
fields.content:
Do this 3x per week:

1. Jumping jacks - 45 sec
2. Squats - 15 reps
3. Pushups - 10 reps
4. Lunges - 10 each leg
5. Plank - 30 sec
6. Glute bridges - 15 reps
7. Bicycle crunches - 20 reps

Rest 30 sec between exercises.
Repeat the whole circuit twice.

Total time: ~15 min. Total burn: real.

fields.title: Stretching and mobility
fields.content:
After every workout, 5 minutes:

- Neck rolls - 30 sec
- Shoulder rolls - 30 sec
- Standing forward fold - 1 min
- Cat-cow - 1 min
- Hip flexor stretch - 30 sec each side
- Hamstring stretch - 30 sec each side

Why: reduces soreness, prevents injury, keeps you moving.

Never stretch cold muscles. Warm up first.

fields.title: Tracking progress
fields.content:
What to track:
- Reps per exercise (should go up)
- Seconds held (planks)
- How you feel (energy, sleep)
- Photos every 4 weeks (subtle changes)

What NOT to track daily: weight (fluctuates too much).
Weigh weekly, same time, same conditions.

Progress isn't linear. Trust the trend.

fields.title: When to rest (and why)
fields.content:
Rest days are when your muscles actually grow.

Signs you need rest:
- Persistent soreness over 3 days
- Can't do a workout you did last week
- Bad sleep, no appetite
- Nagging joint pain

Rest = 1-2 full days/week minimum.
Walk, stretch, hydrate, sleep.

More is not better. Recovery is the workout.

fields.title: What community organizing is
fields.content:
It's helping a group of people solve a shared problem - together.

Not: doing everything yourself
Not: telling people what to do
Not: politics (though it overlaps)

It's: bringing people together, building power, and winning change.

You don't need permission. You need a problem and a few neighbors.

fields.title: Start with one issue
fields.content:
Don't try to fix everything. Pick ONE thing.

Examples:
- The streetlight on our road has been broken for 6 months
- Our school has no clean water
- Women in our area have no safe transport at night
- Our market has no waste collection

Specific. Local. Solvable.

One win → momentum → next bigger win.

fields.title: Find your first 3 people
fields.content:
You don't need a crowd. You need 3 committed people.

Look for:
- The person who already complains about this issue
- Someone with a different skill than you
- Someone with more connections than you

Invite them for tea. Explain the problem. Ask: "Will you help?"

3 is the magic number. From there, growth is easy.

fields.title: Hold your first meeting
fields.content:
Keep it simple and short (60 min):

1. Welcome + why we're here (5 min)
2. Everyone introduces themselves (10 min)
3. Define the problem clearly (15 min)
4. Brainstorm solutions (20 min)
5. Pick ONE action + who owns it (10 min)

Rules:
- Everyone speaks
- No blaming
- End with a specific next step and date

Snacks help. Seriously.

fields.title: Map your power
fields.content:
Before you act, understand:

- Who has the power to fix this? (government, company, landlord)
- What do they care about? (votes, money, reputation)
- Who influences them? (media, donors, community leaders)
- What do you have? (numbers, votes, media attention, money)

You win by understanding who decides and what moves them.

fields.title: Different tactics
fields.content:
Pick based on your situation:

- Petition (public pressure, easy to start)
- Meeting with decision-maker (formal, direct)
- Public demonstration (media attention)
- Social media campaign (youth-friendly, viral)
- Boycott (economic pressure)
- Legal action (slow but powerful)
- Direct action (sits, marches - high risk, high reward)

Most campaigns use 3+ tactics. Combine them.

fields.title: Using social media for change
fields.content:
Build a simple online presence:

- WhatsApp group (for your core team)
- Facebook page (for public visibility)
- Twitter/X (for press + officials)
- Instagram (for youth + visuals)
- TikTok (for short videos of actions)

Post: photos, videos, clear asks, updates.
Hashtag: #OurStreetOurLight #FixOurRoad + your community.

Tag officials publicly. Silence is compliance.

fields.title: Handling opposition and burnout
fields.content:
Two things will happen. Plan for both.

Opposition:
- Some will call you troublemakers (ignore or invite them to see the problem)
- Officials will delay (document everything)
- People will quit (fine - the work continues)

Burnout:
- Rotate roles so no one does everything
- Celebrate small wins
- Take breaks - this is a marathon, not a sprint
- Bring new people in regularly

The goal is a movement, not a hero.

fields.title: Measuring success
fields.content:
Wins aren't always total.

Success levels:
- Full win: the problem is solved
- Partial win: part of the problem solved
- Procedural win: officials agree to talk
- Awareness win: more people know
- Capacity win: your group got stronger

Count them all. Momentum builds on small wins.

fields.title: Sustaining the movement
fields.content:
After your first win - what next?

1. Celebrate publicly (thank everyone)
2. Document what worked (for next time)
3. Keep the group alive (monthly meetups)
4. Pick the next issue (bigger now)
5. Train new leaders (so it's not all on you)

Communities change when ordinary people organize.
You just became one of them.

StepUp exists so you can teach others to do the same.
